dims: The months are lunar: the text keeps them by the new moon and never says how many days a month has, or how the year kept pace with the harvest. The dial draws twelve equal months of thirty days, a schematic, so a day's place on it is approximate.
Abib, the month of the going out, is the first month of the year, drawn at the top; the year runs clockwise.

WEB numbers most dates and names a month only now and then. The fourth and fifth months have no name; Elul is never numbered, and is the sixth by the later calendar. “About March–April” and the rest are the usual equivalents, not the text's.

The flood dates imply thirty-day months but do not state them: the waters came on the 17th day of the 2nd month, prevailed 150 days, and the ship rested on the 17th day of the 7th month: five months for 150 days.

Gold marks the three pilgrim feasts. The feast of weeks has no date: it is counted fifty days from the sheaf, whose own day is “the next day after the Sabbath”, so both are drawn dashed where the count puts them.
Solid where the text ties it to a month or a feast; faded and dashed where the text names only the season, placed by convention.

A filled dot where the text gives the day, a hollow one near the month's middle, clear of the dated days, where it gives only the month; dots on one day stack outward. Where Kings and Jeremiah give different days, the dot is Kings' and the label gives both. Their colours are the stories, and the labels show as you zoom in.
